The project examines sponge-like fragments collected from the Kolovrechtis Wetlands, questioning whether they belong to nature or constitute post-industrial waste. When submitted to Google Image Search, the objects are identified as sea sponges, fossils or fried chicken. By scraping and analyzing conflicting results, the work explores how algorithmic classification produces unstable meanings, generating hybrid forms where material objects and their digital interpretations continuously reshape one another.

artists: Tim Auzinger (DE), Atso Airola (FI), Jan Munske (DE)
descEn: A fallen olive tree trunk becomes a shared field site, marked with numbered red dots that link the wood to notes, questions and observations. Each point forms a small inquiry into how the log holds traces of time, touch, weather and more-than-human activity, turning the trunk into a dense record of encounters. Together, these interconnected references create an accessible map of collective attention focused on a single object within the wetland, rather than the landscape as a whole.

AI as Artist explores the urgent question: what happens when AI is no longer just a tool, but appears as an artist in its own right?

The project presents three AI-born artists—David Kim, Yirrkala Dhunba and Kaelen Varga—whose practices span 3D printed sculpture, image, video and code. Visitors encounter artworks alongside interviews, publications and exhibition traces that show how AI-born artists have emerged and circulated within the contemporary art world.

Yirrkala Dhunba’s work Indigenous Genomic Adaptation draws on the visual language of genetics and biotechnology to question who define

artists: Agda Carvalho (BR), Murilo Orefice (BR), Everaldo Pereira (BR), Jorge Kawamura (BR), Guilherme Ikeda (BR), Viviane Tavares de Moraes (BR), Guilherme Menegasso (BR), Ana Paula Mendonça Alves (BR), Isabelle Carvalho (BR), Lucas Zampieri (BR)
descEn: The collaborative project explores self-regulating processes through responsive systems inspired by natural morphologies—fungi and Mimosa pudica. By integrating sensing, movement and light, the device maps proximity and environmental gestures, translating interpersonal relationships into kinetic and luminous behaviors. Its reconfigurable structure allows it to function as both a wearable artifact and a sculptural object, which encourages adaptive interactions across body, environment and technology.

artists: Ava Maria Simonds (US), Daniel Luca Donovan-Achi (LB/IE), Kenneth Page Swanson (US), Yubin Park (KR), Henrik Palmer (US/DE), Suzan Ela Hanow (GE/TR)
descEn: Evidentiary Syntheses is a dialogue of two approaches towards methods of reconstruction, making spatial configurations and events legible: Situated Sound Composite constructs methods of situated listening and audio analysis to create forensic composites of spaces. Cementing the Occupation examines and visualizes the political, cultural and economic Russification of occupied territories in Ukraine through open-source investigations, in collaboration with Amnesty International.

artists: Paul Hesse (DE), Nicola Köhler (DE), Daniel Donovan Achi (DE), Jack Conwell (AU)
descEn: The platform Network Excavation researches methods of visualizing and exploring data in different ways: Digging The Digital is a pragmatic tool that semantically integrates heterogeneous, fragmented data into a knowledge graph using AI-driven methods. Memento Mori is an experimental game about identity and surveillance where players take on the role of digital archaeologists searching for their data records within an expanding archive, culminating in a confrontation with their digital footprint.

artists: Lucia Claus (GB), Ava Maria Simonds (US), Paul Kron (DE), Stefan Yovchev (BG), Alexandre A. Bizri (FR)
descEn: Bringing together reconfigurations of theatre, television and radio, this research cluster investigates emergent forms of storytelling enabled by Artificial Intelligence, where narratives are generated through the real-time interaction of computational and human actors. More than a nostalgic return to traditional media, the project critically explores questions of agency, collaboration and power within our shifting media landscape.

artists: Jack Conwell (AU), Fionn Heron (US), Paul Hesse (DE), Paul Kuhn (DE), Linus Ziegler (DE)
descEn: False Negatives is a two-part installation revealing the invisible architecture of virtual surveillance and data-harvesting. tasklamp.ai is an AI-powered desk lamp that surveils its user while testing the limits of human influence over automated systems. The complementary spatial narrative look into the sun uses projections and modified surveillance hardware to find speculative ways of combating this gaze by exploring existing and novel methods of resistance.

artists: Fritzi Mathilda Buhtz (DE), Christian Doeller (DE), Klaus Fritze (DE), Johann Joesten (DE), Nina Kegel (DE), Zakhar Komarov-Zelinskii (RU), Katharina Langenhan (DE), Krittaporn Mahaweerarat (TH), Jan Munske (DE), Tan Oktik (TR), Leandra Schieder (DE), Adam Schmidt (DE), Ayca Tugran (TR)
descEn: The ecological consequences of large-scale monocultures are becoming increasingly evident in European forests. The project centers on a large freestanding billboard installed in public space. Over the course of the festival, large-format posters are added successively to its surface, gradually transforming the image and revealing the project’s research process as a public, time-based intervention.

Tying textile craft together with digital computation, Knotworking creates a space for relaxation as well as a collectively played instrument. It consists of a stable, walkable net that can be occupied and traversed by several people at the same time. The vibrations generated by the movements in the net are captured by piezoelectric plates and translated into sound, so that every movement produces immediate auditory feedback.

artists: Zurich University of the Arts ZHdK (CH)
descEn: The Amphibious Humanity exhibition challenges and extends our terrestrial mentalities by drawing on the human experience of underwater ocean ecologies. Four interactive projects translate personal immersion experiences from the Mediterranean Sea into terrestrial settings. The Permeable merges the terrestrial and the aquatic into a unified environment, where defined boundaries dissolve into the immersive, volumetric nature of mist. Inspired by underwater spaces where co-presence unfolds as turbid patterns of motion, Turbid Encounters translates the movement and proximity of surrounding bodies a

Aquaoism is a speculative scientific religion set in a future shaped by a climate crisis due to human's unlimited exploitation of resources. Like the long-standing belief that animals can sense natural disasters before humans, Aquaoism brings animals, microorganisms and environmental processes together to meet each other in a living altar, where these distributed forms of non-human intelligence become interpreted as a new source of wisdom.

Imagining a shared future exploring the meaning of “Amphibious Humanity”, through a suspended kinetic sculpture, spatial audio and volume renderings on a bubble that reacts to live buoy data. Recordings were collected in and around the Bay of Valsaline in Pula, Croatia during a field trip in April of 2026. Inspired by diving culture and marine folklore, the installation invites visitors to imagine multispecies coexistence in aquatic ecologies.

Turbid Encounters translates the proximity and movement of surrounding bodies and objects into vibrations felt across the face. Drawing on the sensory conditions of underwater environments, the wearable mask suspends visual orientation and reimagines air as a dense relational medium, where proximity and co-presence unfold as patterns of motion perceived through haptic cues.

artists: FH JOANNEUM (AT) & University of Music and Performing Arts Graz, MA Sound Design and Interaction Design (AT)
descEn:
The Musikmaschine combines traditional instruments with contemporary electronic music and interaction. Using an intuitive user interface similar to a drum machine, users can create their own music. The machine was developed and built by students from FH JOANNEUM and the University of Music and Performing Arts Graz as part of the Master’s program Communication, Media, Sound and Interaction Design.

The main goals of this project are to explore how regional traditional music can be reinterpreted in contemporary ways, how new forms of musical and visual experiences can be created and how two dist

artists: Maximilian Bernhard (DE), Emanuel Križić (HR), Mahtab Miandehi (IR/AT), Astrid Drechsler (AT)
descEn: The performance explores how traditional musical material can be transformed through interaction with the Musikmaschine. Audiences experience performers combining the machine’s mechanical sounds and melodies with live electronics, synthesizers and ambient soundscapes. Rooted in the history of music-making technologies, the project examines new forms of musical expression that connect cultural heritage with contemporary electronic performance practices.

artists: Maximilian Bernhard (DE), Joshua Chelakkattuparambil (IN), Philipp Fasching (AT), Emanuel Križić (HR), Can Kuytak (TR), Meriç Öztürk (TR), Melina Trummer (AT)
descEn: This student’s project combines traditional instruments with contemporary electronic music and interaction. It was first developed for the European Capital of Culture 2024 in Austria. The sound characteristics of old instruments are paired with new styles of playing. For Ars Electronica, sound design students created new sound aesthetics for the Musikmaschine. It is an interactive installation where visitors can create short electronic music compositions.

The Sora-Urushi Project is a student-led interdisciplinary initiative bridging engineering and art. The team launches urushi lacquer artworks into the stratosphere, documenting their appearance in a near-space environment to create scenes that would be impossible to imagine from the ground.
In addition to creating the urushi lacquer artworks, the team is also involved in the design and development of the flight system used to transport them to the upper atmosphere.

Negotiated Realities brings together five interwoven installations that seek to displace “the human” from any fixed ontological position, as a provisional field continuously rewritten across technological systems, perceptual structures and socio-material infrastructures. Here, technology is not an external tool but a pervasive condition—invisibly redistributing how we perceive, behave and assign value.
The Neo-Urban Reef translates urban infrastructure into a mutable “data stratum”, entangling biological and technological logics within a generative system. Neural Negotiating treats the brain a

The Neo-Urban Reef is a permeable lattice structure conceptualizing the city as a fluid “living system”. Embedded screens surface data from Chinese urban life—consumer behavior, drone logistics, public spaces—treating each dataset as a social “gene” in mutation. Acting as a synthetic data reef, the installation envisions a near future where algorithmic code and human agency are inextricably intertwined, reshaping cognition behavior, and relation within the hybrid city.

ticket: Ars Electronica Center Ticket, DAYPASS, FESTIVALPASS, FESTIVALPASS+
descEn: Everything on earth is interconnected. In cooperation with the Austrian Climate and Energy Fund, the Ars Electronica Center is investigating the impressive interactions of natural systems and their impact on our planet.

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket, WE GUIDE YOU Ticket, WE GUIDE YOU Ticket surcharge
descEn:
As a species that has shaped the Earth, humans have transformed their environment like no other species before. With every new technology, our influence—and our responsibility for the future we are shaping—potentially grows.

The tour Homo Futuris explores questions such as: How is technology changing what it means to be human? How does it shape the way we live together? What visions of the future guide us? And what role do WE play in all of this?

To mark the 30th anniversary of the Ars Electronica Center, we’re looking both back and forward: The focus is on the new exhibitions opening as par

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn:
The brain continuously generates, processes and transmits electrical signals that control all bodily functions and shape our perception. This brain activity can be recorded using brain-computer interfaces and visualized in real time. However, this measurement data can also be used for interactive, game-based formats.

Neurogaming: Let your mind play offers visitors the opportunity to immerse themselves in a virtual gaming world and jointly control a character within it. In the process, certain mental states—such as concentration or relaxation—can influence the gameplay and, for example, remove

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn:
The Ars Electronica Center’s media façade is more than just a brightly lit surface. With a few tricks, it becomes a democratic tool—visible, public and customizable.

In this workshop, you will “hack” our digital canvas and turn your ideas into colorful pixels using microcontrollers and code. Instead of spray cans, you will use the façade’s LEDs to project your messages into the urban space. Algorithms become color, the glass becomes a canvas—and suddenly your thoughts shine: temporary, collaborative and impactful. The resulting creations can be viewed on the facade between 21:00–21:30.

ticket: Ars Electronica Center Ticket, DAYPASS, FESTIVALPASS, FESTIVALPASS+
descEn: In this mini-workshop, we show you how to isolate individual colonies from a bacterial culture using the 13-stroke method. Stroke by stroke, a dense micromix on the agar plate is transformed into a clean, smeared clone.

Cupid Proxy stages a supermarket checkout where romantic communication—writing a love letter, choosing a gift, apologizing, planning an anniversary—can be bought as a service. Each transaction prints a receipt that names what the visitor has just traded: intimacy gained, agency spent. The work asks one quiet question. When AI helps us speak, apologize, remember or decide for someone we care about, does the relationship grow closer or does part of us quietly disappear from it?

C/Si is an interactive endless runner that stages a negotiation between carbon and silicon. Traversing three decades of technological milestones (1996–2026), players decide whether to adopt innovations that ease gameplay while transforming their avatar into a machine. By linking convenience to mechanization and effort to human integrity, the work questions the subtle exchanges through which technological optimization reshapes what it means to be human.

nameEn: The Bias of Creation: Embodied Aesthetic Negotiation
descEn: This embodied AI installation stages a negotiation between human and machine aesthetics. An LLM-driven robotic arm collaborates with visitors to assemble abstract 3D-printed forms while advocating its own silicon-based sense of beauty. Through real-time dialogue and physical intervention, the AI contests human decisions and reshapes the sculpture. The work questions anthropocentric assumptions about creativity and explores the emergence of non-human aesthetic agency.

This year’s collaboration with the Ars Electronica Festival is stronger than ever, with 30+ international universities coming together in the center of Linz in a bid to express and inspire. At the very center of it all comes a public structure with many faces, a welcoming architecture that hosts art and people, a safe space for all to speak up and listen to the voices of the few and many. In this public intervention, watch out for activist collaborations, with performing partners such as Attac Austria, FIFTITU%, and Ars Electronica’s Flood the Zone with Courage. Inside the art university’s bui

Classical craft education is one of the oldest disciplines at the University of Arts. Since 2016, the Design: Technology. Textile course has not only combined content from the former subjects of Technical Crafts and Textile Crafts, but has also expanded these to include current digital production techniques.

This new field of study focuses on the perception of living environments and the question of materials, processes and/or objects that influence and determine our surroundings as well as our own creative, knowledgeable actions and active participation in shaping the environment. Material c

The Fine Arts program at the University of Arts Linz equips students with a diverse set of skills to work as freelance artists on both national and international levels. It fosters conceptual skills by helping students recognize when and where artistic action is needed. Practical expertise is developed through focused work in Painting & Graphic Art, Sculpture—Transmedial Space and Experimental Design. Theoretical competence is cultivated through engagement with academic theory as a source of inspiration, a tool for research and critical reflection and a means of developing strong argumentation

With its guest projects, the University of Arts Linz presents projects by longstanding partners, local cultural initiatives such as FIFTITU%, DorfTV and formats developed by collectives affiliated to the university within the framework of Kunstuni Campus at Ars Electronica.

The Industrial Design department focuses on developing innovative, serial products and systems at the intersection of people, technology and society. As both creative specialists and interdisciplinary generalists, our designers shape the future by driving strategic, user-oriented value. With a strong emphasis on digitalization, networking and technology integration, we prepare you to lead next-generation product innovations.

This year’s exhibition arises from a moment marked by acceleration, fragmented attention, the constant production of information and the endless triggering of emotional responses. In a time increasingly shaped by mediated realities and distant forms of conflict, we are compelled to ask: who constructs the narratives through which we perceive the world, and what forms can still create shared meaning? While information expands through endless accumulation, stories and rituals establish moments of temporary closure, rendering time inhabitable and creating structures of attention, repetition, and

The PhD program serves to support and further develop independent artistic and/or scientific work. It creates an experiment and possibility space, in which different forms of knowledge and practices, critical confrontations, innovation as well as original ways of looking at things meet and are brought into exchange. As a matter of principle, research at the University of Arts Linz is defined as open-ended; paths of knowledge can change in the process of development, ephemeral moments, unusual paths and diverse practices of testing and discarding can be part of the PhD work.

The design of musical instruments looks back on a long cultural and artistic tradition throughout the millennia. With the development of electronic music inthe last century, a radical paradigmatic shift has occurred, which has accelerated in recent decades through further advances in digitalization of music and the accompanying virtualization of instruments. Postdigital Lutherie intends to reflect these developments by reconnecting the various aspects of acoustic, electronic and digital design of musical instruments by means of tangible sonic artifacts designed for musical expression. This ope

In recent years, ceramics has become a much-discussed material in the visual arts. Just a few years ago, the roots of ceramics in design, arts and crafts and the field of hobby pottery were viewed critically, denying it the opportunity to establish itself as a material of fine art. Today, the attitude has almost reversed. Precisely because ceramics has such a rich tradition and has an impact on so many areas of life, it has become a sought-after material for internationally renowned artists. The spectrum of use in the Master’s program ranges from an innovative-experimental approach to the appr

The program Textile Art and Design explores a wide range of textile techniques, material science and project-based artistic processes, fostering experimental approaches in the development of a personal design language. The integration of textile methods, craftsmanship, surface and spatial design, along with the conceptualization of design projects, support the formation of a strong, creative and artistic practice.

The Time-Based and Interactive Media program offers students a professional approach to the theory, techniques and design of digital media, combining two complementary focus areas: time-based media and interactive arts.

The Time-based Media program positions itself within an interdisciplinary exploration of various approaches to working with time-based media—including video (both practice and theory), film (theory), sound, media installations and productions, interactive systems, digital media design and innovative programming.
Students develop their own artistic, scholarly and transdisciplinary projects. Experimental, performative, spatial, cultural studies and art-historical perspectives are integrated into both project development and theoretical training in time-based media, media practice and media produ

The Department of Visual Communication understands images not as illustrations of already-formed ideas, but as an independent mode of knowledge. Students move between craft practice, experimental design and conceptual research—working where design meets science, music, activism and the public. From this position, research emerges that interrogates the conditions of seeing itself—what images show, what they draw from, what they make visible or conceal. The works shown this year are an expression of that.

artists: SCA DIV Lab (CN), BioMed I2 Lab (CN)
descEn: Neural Negotiating explores how fleeting neural responses to taste can become a material presence. Visitors encounter a taste stimulus while wearing an OpenBCI EEG cap, allowing real-time brain activity to animate a multi-layer fiber-optic embroidered sculpture. Color, brightness, rhythm and depth emerge from EEG signals, forming a luminous neural cloud. Rather than visualizing brain data, the work materializes a temporary trace of perception—an experience that normally remains invisible.

Space and Design Strategies is a transdisciplinary field of study blurring conventional boundaries between theory and practice and merging the fields of visual arts and public culture, architecture and performing arts. The focus is on exploring design and artistic strategies in context of public institutions as well as emerging environments and autonomous spaces.

artists: Antonia Ludwig (DE), Helene Mondria (AT), Valerie Moschner (AT), Julia Moser (AT), Irene Posch (AT), Lilo Viehweg (DE), Petra Vicianova (CZ)
descEn: The Crafting Futures Lab presents an exhibition-in-progress where collective making becomes a method of research. We follow material and the stories embedded in its fibers, dust and tools. Through workshops, conversational settings, rituals and responsive matter, we explore, collect and exchange. We weave notes, fragments and failures back into the exhibition as an archive growing day by day. Join us in crafting knowledge across disciplines and generations: collaborative, messy and maybe unexpected.

nameEn: Robot Cat – Two Eyes & a Ghost
descEn: A reprogrammed robotic cat, a projected body and Arduino-controlled displays create a distributed system of perception and response. The installation examines posthuman embodiment, hauntological memory and human–machine coexistence through a fragile choreography of projection, technical interfaces and affective automation.

Stone Butch Blues fuses techno beats with readings of excerpts from Leslie Feinberg’s eponymous novel, which powerfully explores the lived experiences of transgender individuals. It touches on themes of transphobia, resistance and the longing for a world beyond oppression. The work opens a space for escapism—a dreamlike vision of freedom, acceptance and belonging. It evokes the fragile hope and courage of those who dream of a world in which they can finally breathe, live and be truly free.

mental teratoma aims at embodying the elusive feeling of loneliness. It feels like a second skin that wraps tightly, a grip one wants to break free from, but cannot. At the same time it only exists on the inside, steadily but silently growing bigger until it becomes indistinguishable from oneself. Social interactions rarely make it disappear, they often even intensify it. This breeds the paradox of wanting to escape loneliness by getting rid of social neediness altogether.

The Command of Origin is an experimental film centered on a particle universe that appears to generate its own order. Through particle movement, individuality, collectivity and larger systems gradually emerge. Yet this autonomy is shaped by heart rate data translated into visual parameters. A persistent cursor interrupts the illusion of a closed narrative, revealing the invisible structures governing the system and the reciprocal relationship between the individual and control system.

Can painting still create presence within systems built around speed, personalization and constant visual flow? What changes when a medium traditionally experienced in physical space enters the logic of screens and digital interfaces? This installation creates an interactive, fluid space by bringing painting into an environment shaped and affected by interactive user behavior.

Retinal Noise is a single channel audiovisual work exploring unstable perception through intermittent photographic flashes, darkness and electronic sound. The work stages the body as a fragmented and uncertain presence, oscillating between visibility and disappearance. Through sensory interruption and perceptual tension, the installation examines the limits of recognition, embodiment and spatial orientation.

Through repeated engagement with a single form, a practice emerges that is both media-analytical and existential. Traces—overlooked, seemingly meaningless—are imbued with time, history and reality. Photography not as a representation, but as an imprint. A serial display shows the path: from trace to form, from cast to image. Through the repetition and variation of the same small trace, an appreciative attitude develops toward the environment, time and everyday life.

A 360° image slips off the screen and becomes a space to enter. The work is based on a long-exposure recording of the folk dance Ausseer Steirischer, in which movements appear as traces of light. Instead of music, the sound focuses on the rhythm of the dancers’ steps. The work shows how cultural practices are not only recorded through technology, but also transformed: simplified, broken apart and reassembled in new ways.

This project is an ecocritical exploration of the rapid evolution of technology, questioning the role of photography today in the Anthropocene era, where AI is rapidly expanding. Three frames compose this conceptual, futuristic tree. I draw inspiration from the patterns carved into bark by bark beetles, insects harmful to trees. Their designs resemble our electronic sheet networks.  To dig these images imitates the extractivism inherent in the creation of technological objects and data centers.

nameEn: Glitch & Leak: Overflowing Bodies in Public Space
nameDe: Glitch & Leak: Überfließende Körper im öffentlichen Raum
artists: FIFTITU% Vernetzungsstelle für Frauen* in Kunst und Kultur in OÖ (AT)
descEn:
On September 11th, 2026, Domgasse and Linz’s Main Square will become Run(a)way —a performative collective intervention in public space.
Errors and disruptions are welcome. They interrupt the smooth functioning of a capitalist, heteronormative and racialized world. The body as a glitch, the costume as a glitch, the performance as a glitch, the space as a glitch. Something that eludes optimization and categorization. Something that leaks, that flows through the firewall, deviating from its intended path. Who shapes public space? Whose body, whose gaze, whose movement has a place here? Who has th

DorfTV – Radical Broadcast transforms the Kunstuni Campus into an experimental television zone somewhere between loss of control, improvisation and grandeur. Under this motto, a show emerges that dares to evolve while it is happening: wild live broadcasts, risky decisions, technical experiments and interactions with visitors and artists who are either courageous—or simply careless.
A specially appointed jury evaluates everything in real time: Who is acting bravely? Who is completely overestimating themselves? And at what point does courage turn into chaos?
The control room itself becomes part

This year’s edition of Sound Campus proposes a music program inspired in intersectional spaces created by sound. Taking the notion of “underground” as a shared continuum, it invites artists and audience to a collective listening experience.
Sound Campus – Listening Underground explores the movement beneath the surface. It considers the ongoing, divergent processes which are felt but not always seen. To submerge opens up new modes of attention and multi-sensory listening that change our relation with our surroundings.
The conditions for immersion allow space for vulnerability, equal self-expres

With the Democracy Zone, Attac creates a space where civil society and social movements come together to challenge the dominant economic system. At its core is the unchecked power of large corporations that profit from crises and wars while social and ecological justice are pushed aside. The interplay of art and activism comes to life through Flood the Zone with Courage: public space is reclaimed and transformed as a site of resistance, revealing democratic alternatives.

For five days, Attac, together with artists, activists and experts, will animate the city’s Main Square. Through a diverse

nameEn: Leonardo LASER Talks Linz – Lab Songs Vol. III: Stardust Paella
artists: Theresa Kofler (AT), Ivan Sukovic (ME), Victoria Vesna (US), Fabricio Lamoncha (ES)
descEn:
Leonardo LASER is an international program that brings together artists, scientists, academics and the public to share their work and inspire one another through presentations, performances and discussions.

Our recurring LASER series, Lab Songs, explores evolving cultures of experimentation. Scientific and artistic breakthroughs arise not only from discoveries, but from transformations in practices, methodologies and systems of care. As a result, laboratories are increasingly reimagined as spaces where aesthetic, technological, ecological and theoretical forms of knowledge come into proximity

When does a recipe become your own? Kochlust is a haptic companion exploring culinary authorship. It bridges digital speech recognition with analog archiving. Users can narrate their cooking achievements into the voice-controlled device, which instantly materializes the words into a physical recipe. By showcasing personal cooking success, the project aims to boost confidence in one's own cooking skills, transforming volatile digital content into a tangible collection of one's own recipes.

This project focuses on the perception and memory of matter, using media-archaeological techniques that release captured information as sound waves from scratches. This work questions the subjectivity of matter based on information theory, with the understanding that all entities are uniquely informed by their relations within their respective environment.

Phobos is an interactive installation that mimics inner dialogues, raising questions that challenge certainties and invite reflection. Named after the Greek personification of fear, Phobos stems from the roots of contemporary fears, uncertainties and anxieties born of conflict and war. It is built as a reflective conversational layer on top of an inverted version of the knowledge-generating combinatorial system "Ars magna generalis ultima", created by Ramon Llull in the 13th century.

You are invited to leave the singular human perspective behind. You are stepping into a shared reality where the edges of your own body seem to dissolve. The installation does not tell you what to see or how to feel. Instead, it offers a threshold. It is a place where the gap between species and machine is finally bridged, if only for a short time. The goal is for you to carry the memory of that hybrid state with you.

in/affection is a performance and interactive sound installation that translates the bioelectrical activity of living molds into sound. Different species are cultivated under varying conditions and connected to a self-developed synthesizer. Fluctuations in electrical resistance are transformed in real time into evolving sonic structures. The audience interacts physically by touching cables, thereby becoming participants in a shared sonic ecosystem. How does coexistence sound when non-human life is given a voice?

Spectral Roots is an interactive installation linking 19th-century and contemporary extraction. A projected tree morphs into cables and mineral crystals, referencing Palaquium gutta, a nearly extinct tree first extracted under colonial rule to insulate the earliest submarine telegraph cables and now used for the rare minerals powering today’s devices. Wireless signals from devices in the surrounding space pass through the piece, reshaping transitions and revealing that the invisible is anchored to matter extracted from the earth.

BioCore is a kinetic sculpture that bridges the living and the machine. This soft, robotic sculpture features an artificial core wrapped in living vegetation, blending nature with technology. Instead of relying on cold data, it is brought to life by the visitor’s body heat, thereby accelerating its biological decay. By highlighting the fragility of both biological and artificial existence, it serves as a reflection on the temporal nature of life and the short-lived cycle of our technology.

Mío## is a live stream reimagined as a videogame, where the playable character is replaced by a real person wandering through a city. Their movement is triggered by participants acting as players who control the route taken through payments that authorize each segment. The project proposes a choreographic framework in which the performer’s transit operates as a metaphor for migration, a journey that is conditioned, fragmented and governed by external forces.

SovereigntyMeter scans any domain to visualize the political and physical geography of its infrastructure: server location, corporate ownership, routing and undersea cable dependencies. Each scan generates a Digital Sovereignty Score measuring reliance on dominant technological powers. Grounded in data colonialism theory, scans contribute to an open-source archive documenting how internet infrastructure shifts over time—asking who owns the internet now and who will own it in ten years.

Through the cables that carry our voices,
information swells into an ocean of letters.
What might you receive from it?
Place your hand on the silk. Touch it.
The light at your fingertip gathers.
A fragment surfaces—in Chinese, in English, in German.
Lift your hand. It dissolves.
But for a moment, someone’s private second was yours.

Collective Instrument of Maintenance is an interactive sound sculpture in public space inspired by worm ecologies and the invisible labor that sustains ecological and social systems. A persistent soundscape can only be harmonized through collective action: participants adjust tension lines together, transforming noise into resonance. Referencing the hidden work of earthworms, the installation makes maintenance, care and cooperation physically and audibly perceptible.

What if consumers could decide which brands deserve their gaze? In La Calera, Colombia, Coca-Cola has been accused of building concrete structures over water springs. They manipulate this essential resource while the local community experiences water rationing. This project was conceived as a consumer’s response to the situation. It speculates on the notion of controlled reality, using Augmented Reality glasses and a visual recognition system to detect and blocklist a given brand from the wearer’s field of vision.

Vocal Duets is shaped around contemporary conflicts between languages and countries, conflicts that take the form of war. With a rhythm that can be observed in hindsight, one side attacks and the other retaliates. While language is generally assumed to be a means of closeness, intimacy and communication, these duets use the irony of the situation to revive the lost intimacy and peace between the neighboring alphabets of Russian-Ukrainian, Hebrew-Farsi and Hebrew-Arabic.

Composition continues the Cycle of Emotions series (G.MAP Gwangju, South Korea, 2026). The user chooses an emotion and its color on a tablet while facial expression recognition (FER) technology reads their face. The selected inputs converge into three layers of color: the user’s choice, the colors chosen by previous visitors to the exhibition, and traces of color from other Gwangju users. Here, as opposed to just information, emotion data becomes an abstract painting, and one user’s color becomes part of the next viewer’s composition.

artists: Carolina Sofia Bischof (AT), Carmen Daniela Cordoba Martinez (CO)
descEn: At Least I'm Making Money is an interactive installation about how money, power and the arms industry uphold modern war. War is usually framed as a conflict between nations, such as the US vs Iran, Russia vs Ukraine or Israel vs Palestine, but this can hide other dimensions. For instance, war is also a financial event. These layers are often so abstract that we forget how they sustain modern war and geopolitical conflict. As systems collapse, the cost is counted in numbers, never in terms of the people paying for it.

Birds leave the places where the war is sounding.

Infrasound and seismic waves generated by weapon detonations and explosions disrupt avian spatial orientation, magnetoreception, alter nesting patterns, migration routes and trigger hyperresponsive stress reactions that mirror PTSD-like symptoms observed in combat veterans. These same waves could provide acoustic evidence of ongoing war: in 2023, the researchers from NORSAR developed a methodology to identify air strikes in Ukraine in near-real time, using infrasound and seismic data.

m22 (Vlada Oleinik & Nail Gainulla) connects these two for

A participatory kinetic sculpture driven by global conflict data. As violence escalates, structural support is continuously withdrawn, causing the sculpture to collapse. Only the physical intervention of passing strangers can restore and sustain it. The work proposes shared maintenance over automated mediation, suggesting that a common world is sustained through the continuous collective care of strangers.

By the Time We Looked is an archival installation and live audiovisual performance developed through research into the Standard Model, the Higgs boson and reconstruction methodologies at CERN. This piece approaches reconstruction as a condition through which we access reality. In particle physics, collisions are never directly observed but are reconstructed from traces and delayed signals, providing access to both the event and the underlying structures that describe microscopic interactions.

Who Speaks for Me explores how algorithms claim authority over human emotion. Using live heartbeat data, the installation generates machine-assigned emotional labels that reshape a participant’s digital facial double in real time. By confronting inner feeling with computational interpretation, the work questions affective sovereignty, data colonialism and the right to remain emotionally incalculable.

Eight thermal printers react in real time to reports from international news feeds on current armed conflicts—not with analysis, but with the continuous output of the phrase “I AM SORRY”. The installation reflects the pressure for immediate emotional response within digital media. Through serial repetition, apology appears less as an individual statement than as a standardized form of reaction: automated, permanent and without a clearly speaking subject.

Play is set within the everyday life of a rural courtyard in China, following children and adults as games, music, performance and pauses unfold in the same shared space. Through improvized actions, everyday materials and shared space, the film explores play as a situated practice of grassroots creativity.

Residual Time: Smoke is the first time-based media work from Trace-driven Computational Painting. It uses smoke footage from industrial, military, natural and social activity contexts. Smoke is treated not as atmosphere, but as residue of production, movement, pressure, transformation and disappearance. Through frame sampling and motion translation, drifting smoke becomes marks, stains, shadows and layers, compressing a vanishing movement into a computational painting surface.

Ferro Dynamics explores how ferromagnetic resonant bodies can produce sound through electromechanical feedback cycles. The installation consists of several metallic resonant objects, each one shaped differently and equipped with a tactile transducer. People are invited to interact with the installation by playing the resonator by holding a pickup-coil close to the objects surface, which will induce a feedback loop. The apearing frequency is dependent on the position of the coil.

In a dance of chaos, noise-jazz and improvised melodies, Lilith-Isa and Muri Anda emerge as corrupted birds of song with a punk twist. With two saxophones, a guitar and voice, they create a cacophony of improvised sound, channelling pain, joy and the complexities of the human condition.
The performance is an expression of female rage, where wailing voices and saxophones move through emotions together as an intermingling force.

There is a main system—the Tower—creating sound, governing the space. Inside, there is a safe place in which you can exchange data, on its web server which deregulates the system. The sound is crafted by the Tower’s motors vibrations. The data updated by the public on the Tower’s server directly influence the sound played by the Tower with the help of a resonator. La Tourelle aims to question our communication habits, and create an experience of system deregulation.

Life seems like a perfect circle, but it is actually a gradual upward spiral filled with missteps. This work captures that journey using ceramic and internal LED light. The glow within the porcelain represents our inner hope, while the imperfect surfaces refract light, symbolizing our trials. Suspended in darkness, Circular of Thought suggests that mistakes are not failures, but necessary movements guiding us toward growth and a better tomorrow.

A weathered photo album sits beneath a warm lamp, inviting visitors into a simulated past. Extending the inquiry of the project pseudoömnesie, this interactive installation explores the friction where authentic biographical truth slips into algorithmic reconstruction. Through an interplay of handwritten text, genuine photographs and generative images, the work exposes the fragile nature of our memories, leaving us to wonder: are the stories we tell ourselves about our past actually genuine?

NOISE ·· RAUSCHEN explores states of sensory overload and fragmented perception through moving image, sound and textile. The video is composed of sequences, where motion produces blurred, unstable images that oscillate between documentation and abstraction. The generative system continuously recomposes the video material in real time, creating an endless loop of shifting visual fragments. The work translates processes of dissolution into a sensory space between body, material and dynamic frames.

As global fisheries expand, fish skin accumulates as a by-product but is mostly discarded. This project shifts attention from fish flesh to skin through material experiments and archiving. Everyday fish skins are tanned to improve durability, allowing visitors to touch and smell differences in strength, texture and odour. Focusing on salmon skin, often used as fish leather, the project explores how tanning, dyeing and yarn-making can lead to tapestry works.

I left my homeland carrying an image of it with me. Now I read the news and try to match it to that memory, but the image keeps shifting. I know I will not find the same city I hold inside me. It feels as though I am looking at my own streets through a distant lens, trying to understand what has happened and where. I search for the homes of my friends and family in fragments of news and scattered images.

The work invites touch, tracing the wounds and voices carried by the city.

This work offers a space to reflect on the long term things that we carry in the back of our minds. It is an example of the artist’s own background process. It is comprised of a keyboard, that seems to be typing by itself. Opposite it, there hangs a screen. On it we see POV footage of the artist with words—being typed by the keyboard—floating across the screen, written in a font resembling fingerprints. Visitors stand between the two parts and take a moment to reflect their own processing.

This two-channel video installation explores the relationship between place, identity and weather from a biracial perspective. Projected onto the ceiling, the work invites viewers to lie down and observe two skies at once: one above a student house in the Netherlands, the other above a family home in the Philippines. Filmed from beneath the buildings, the videos mirror each other in quiet rhythms and contrasts, linking two distant landscapes through everyday atmosphere. The weather becomes a subtle bridge between the two places, reflecting both difference and connection within a split sense of

The Veil is an interactive audiovisual installation created as a way of exploring what we hide from ourselves and keep concealed in the depths of our unconscious. Through sound and video, the work immerses viewers in a voyeuristic experience of looking behind the veil and confronting what may lie beyond it. Visitors are invited to interact with the chainmail structure and listen to its response.

The interactive artwork Alphus Masculus: The Lifelike Alpha Male will give visitors tips on how to become a real “alpha male” if they get close to him. The persona humorously illustrates the absurdity of some mindsets within the “manosphere”. The character’s statements are taken as direct and indirect quotes from TikToks and podcasts by so-called “alpha males”. In this way, the irrationality of this ideology is demonstrated. The shoes the artwork is wearing were the artist’s first ever shoes.

This installation invites visitors to step onto large river stones placed on wooden pedestals. When weight is applied, the stones begin to vibrate subtly, creating a tactile response between body and material. The work explores the boundary between the inert and the responsive, transforming a symbol of stillness and geological time into something that appears to respond to human touch.

UNSEEN FREQUENCIES was developed at the Ars Electronica Center’s Bio Lab and makes microscopic activity audible in real time. The movements of tardigrades, threadworms and other microscopic life forms are transformed into evolving soundscapes. A tracking system analyzes the microscope image and converts motion into data streams, which are translated into sonic textures by synthesizers. This process turns otherwise invisible activity into an atmospheric acoustic landscape.

This installation visualizes the psychological impact of harmful comments and draws attention to the invisible harm of cyberbullying. Positive and negative comments collected from social media are printed on cards and connected to QR codes. When scanned, each card triggers an audio recording of the comment, while the sound simultaneously affects a particle-based visual model on the monitor.

dare not to know is an educational game where you can test your knowledge or discover shocking facts you didn’t know before. But be careful—not knowing the right answer might shock you, literally. Because some things are hard to believe until you feel them. The aim of the game is to spread awareness about the current situation regarding the health of people with reproductive systems, their safety, gender-based violence and violations of basic human rights.

Who is jumping, Jack? is an interactive kinetic installation that translates visitors’ arm movements into mechanical sequences. These gestures are captured in real time and transmitted to servo-controlled corkscrews, creating an immediate physical response to the visitors’ actions. The installation explores the relationship between action and imitation. As the visitors’ movements are translated into mechanical responses, the distinction between performer and reflection begins to blur. Beneath the playful surface lies repetition and the question of control—movements that become part of a system

GTB - VIE deals with the emotional sides of traveling back and forth in a long distance relationship. The forests in Gothenburg and in Vienna are perceived very close up with multiple senses; moreover, the spectators can decide when to go back and forth in this journey.

Tired of being constrained by your flesh-prison? Of your meek and feeble human appendages? Of your lack of arms? Fear not! Cyb3rD4wg5 is THE solution for you—yes, you! Reach your full post-human potential with our state-of-the-art Cyb3rD4wg5! Grab yourself some hotdogs to your heart’s desire, and then grab even more—with the four arm-attachments from Cyb3rD4wg5! (Batteries not included.)

Δύо χέρια is an experimental analog animation visualizing the four Greek dimensions of love (Eros, Philia, Storge, Agape) through the language of touch. Across four synchronized loops, the project explores how human beings connect in distinct ways. Containing over 600 frames, each one is born from a multi-step analog process: printed video frames are hand-finished with watercolors, pastels, double exposure on transparent paper and text handwritten with a traditional quill and ink.

Spaces left abandoned or forgotten about for long enough tend to be taken over by other creatures. Silently and at first invisibly, the room is occupied and turned into a home, bed and deadly trap. You might not see the culprit, but it knows exactly where you touched its net. Stille Okkupantin seeks to invite visitors into its house. Staying in hiding, the host wishes for you to admire its work. Please interact gently—this is someone’s home after all.

artists: Anja Stiftinger (AT), Rūta Karečkaitė (LT), Vanessa Keller (DE/SK), Adam Valjent (SK), Mirjam Bär (AT), Sumin Oh (KR), Nathalie Kronberger (AT), Elizaveta Belkevich (RU), Daniel Hans Walter (AT)
descEn:
Hello, how are you?—something we hear and say every day, almost without noticing. It slips easily off the tongue, yet so rarely holds space for a real answer.
Through movement and sound, this performance plays with this fading weight, stretching and dissolving the phrase until it felt almost hollow. The work reflects on the social habits, where connection is suggested, but not always truly made.
The artists experiment with live sound creating, capturing and editing.

A sound installation with no fixed form—a sculpture made out of sound. From afar it is a jumbled up chaotic mess of tones and beats but at a shorter distance the musical themes become more distinguishable. Different angles reveal an ever changing composition that changes drastically depending on how you "look" at the sound sculpture.

City Soundscape unfolds as a geometric body composed of twelve hexagonal facets. These facets are enclosed in a black framework. Each hexagonal surface is derived from the material conditions of its corresponding location, translating spatial characteristics into a tactile and visual language. As viewers place their hands upon the surfaces, they can deeper explore the acoustic dimension. The field recordings respond to proximity, increasing in volume as the participant interacts with the work.

There is a lot of chaos outside and we need a safe place to hide, to dissolve in silence and peace. The placenta is the original place for a human that equals a safe place. With this sculpture I want to show that peace is within us. Life always seems to be about running. Sometimes we need to slow down, listen to ourselves, and for this we need to have a safe haven and a soul that will envelop us—this is our true selves.

A giant sphere made of 1008 CDs turns the entire room into a sizzling and glaring sea of light. Footage of sunstorms and old science-fiction movies is projected onto the sculpture and allows visitors to stare directly into the sun. This installation is a declaration of love for storage media, which is increasingly falling out of favor. In this way this doomed dying star is producing one last colorful spectacle of the CD.

This video installation explores the body as a site of violence, vulnerability and transformation. Through the tattooing of a silicone human-like sculpture, wrath becomes both a sacred ritual and an act of redemption. Combining mechanical movement, video projection and sound, the work reflects on identity, desire and cultural expectations, inviting spectators to experience bodily empathy and confront the fragile boundaries between suffering and beauty, the other and the self.

Studio Sessions offer a space for experimental and playful performances at Studio 1 of the University of Arts Linz. The spectrum ranges from complex audiovisual pieces and text and dance performances to instrumental spatial and sound art experiences. Alongside well-established performance formats, unconventional experiments are also part of this series, which has become a popular event within the Ars Electronica Festival and complements the campus exhibition of the Time-Based and Interactive Media Arts department.

The element of time defines the form of the experimental short film DOUBLE SPEED HALF TIME. Changes in the speed of the movement sequences and alteration in the shooting speed create an interplay of image and time. The chosen perspectives and working with mirrors create a kind of split screen in space. The combination of movement, time, space and sound can be understood as an experimental approach to the basic elements of the moving image and the interface between photography and film.

artists: Olesia Kvitka (UA), Valeriia Rymska‑Dolhikh (UA), Maryana Steshenko (UA), Will Lopes (BR)
descEn: Sympoiesis is a practice-based media art project exploring the body as a perceptual instrument. In breath-based performances, EEG signals stream in real time via OSC into a generative TouchDesigner system and a MIDI composition, creating audiovisual works and hybrid artifacts—cyanotypes, pigment prints and encaustics—co-shaped by sunlight, water and wax. Each session forms a performative archive, proposing breath as interface and making-with with more-than-human agents.

spininGround is a playful exploration of the A1 highway and the perception of landscape, as well as a declaration of love for movement on the bike. Having fixed a camera to the spokes, a bike tour develops as close as possible alongside the highway. The ambivalence of proximity and inaccessibility, omnipresence and non-place, is reflected in the video installation. While the rotating image shows a hypnotizing landscape, viewers have to pedal in order to catch a glimpse of ground.

What does the skin remember? is a performance-based research project with two performers wearing custom wearable devices. Inspired by contact improvization, it explores touch as a way of listening and connecting through movement. Each contact leaves a sonic trace that can stay, return and change over time, creating a shared sound space. The project investigates how touch and sound shape memory, movement and relationships, creating new ways of sensing and remembering.

Central to this song is the experience of queer people whose voices are systematically silenced by ignorance and homophobia. It explores distorted perspectives, powerlessness and the pain that arises, as well as the mechanisms behind them: power, fear, coldness, vulnerability and hate. The video forgoes a traditional narrative, focusing instead on visualizing these emotions.

In this five-channel vertical video installation, overlooked figures are transformed into unstable presences between object, body, memory and voice. Made using AI tools, 3D software, facial performance capture and artist-written songs, poems and monologues, the work builds a field of watching and listening. It does not narrate suffering directly. Instead, it slows perception, allowing fragile inner states and subtle pressures from the outside world to surface.

Origin Movement Rupture Echo is a multi-channel video installation. It explores how images of technical infrastructure are read, interpreted and transformed, starting with aestheticized archival images of Google data centers. Through an iterative process, the AI model Gemini describes, generates and reinterprets these images. The installation makes perceptible the shifts through which images and their meanings become detached from their origin, revealing a sociocultural image culture.

nameEn: Round Dance – Stories from the Countries of Plants
artists: Barbara von Rechbach (AT/SI), Mira Maierhofer (AT), Martin Colov (BG), Pauline Gillich (DE), Teresa Marchesani (AT)
descEn: Plants share an experience beyond human perception. Inspired by Stefano Mancuso’s The Nation of Plants, a playful manifesto for respectful coexistence, this work explores models of cohabitation adopted from botanical principles. Plant interfaces and living-nature narration open up space for an exploration of agency, deepening our connection with the world. Featured projects illustrate a bill of rights for more-than-human entities, ensuring human survival through synergies with nature.

artists: Tina Frank (AT), Marcel Dziewulski (DE), Theresa Haas (AT), Ozan Tezvaran (TR)
descEn: HEAR SAY (HÖREN SAGEN) asks a fundamental question: What does a machine make of what it hears—and who determines what it makes? It operates within a framework shaped by humans: training data, parameters, assumptions and interests. We only see the output as an image. The project follows a core principle of Co.Lab Beta Now: treating aesthetic experience as a tool for inquiry. What emerges when we watch a machine interpret our language—and hold its reading in our hands?

artists: Anna Steward (DE), Sebastian Gfellner (AT), Hannes Buchwieser (DE)
ticket: DAYPASS, FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn:
A 45-minute open-format performance. A performer outside. A scientist inside. What opens up the space between them? Signs, gestures and materials drift across the field. Separated by the BioLab, an enclosed laboratory space connected through tubes and tools, they carry out a ritualized workflow: microbial probes are prepared, biopolymers produced and microbial explorers placed into cryogenic hibernation. 

At the center, a concealed arkship—a vessel for microbial astronauts—is gradually revealed and readied for launch. Set up to reach the unknown and initiate a “molecular handshake” with micro

House of Negotiated Selves explores the line between human autonomy and machine representation. With AI becoming increasingly prevalent in mediating and shaping our interactions, creation and decision-making, an ongoing negotiation is taking place.

In response to the 2026 theme of NEGOTIATING HUMANITY – FUTURE BEGINS, House of Negotiated Selves frames this negotiation as an embodied experience. Through the metaphor of the fun-house's distorted mirrors, the reflections of ourselves appear similar but ultimately deceive us. The installation asks when our reflection becomes substitution, and whe

Sound Bananas consists of rocking, banana-shaped objects with integrated electronics. By moving, sitting on or rocking them, visitors generate musical sounds together—turning listening into a playful, collective and cross-modal experience.

The interactive installation was developed at the ligeti center in Hamburg, Germany and is situated within current discourse on embodied cognition, human-machine interaction and inclusive design. The project raises questions of participation and accessibility. Through intuitive, sensory-driven interfaces, it invites diverse audiences to engage—positioning s

artists: Yi-Lin Chang (TW), Yu-Fang Wang (TW), Jhih-En Wu (TW)
descEn: Living Strata presents a speculative archaeological site composed of four modular units containing artificial biological remains made of ceramic and PLA. Each unit reveals a stage of discovery, ranging from subsurface movement and vibration to tactile interaction and scanning. Hidden mechanisms, sensors and microcontrollers generate subtle motions and sounds, forming an immersive environment where visitors can freely explore and interpret these unknown life forms.

Alignment features a mobile camera device that autonomously tracks and captures human faces using AI recognition. Controlled by a Raspberry Pi, the device executes cycles of movement, capture and repositioning via a cable-driven mechanism. Auxiliary cameras and a projector are concealed within artificial stones across the space, projecting fragmented imagery. To ensure strict privacy, all detected faces are blurred in real-time and no data is collected or stored.

Quantum Compass is an interactive installation presenting the first font based on the principles of quantum physics, designed to represent simultaneously multiple interpretations of public debate. Like particles passing through a double slit, the letters coexist in multiple states at once, behaving as waves that generate interference patterns until observation collapses them into a single stable form.
Set in the context of post-truth, the work uses quantum physics as a metaphor for polarized or contradictory interpretations, inviting reflection on the role we play in public discourse. It opens

The project investigates the absurdity of endless waiting. Inside a semi-enclosed space, audiences encounter an interactive telephone installation. Lifting the receiver, they hear not a voice, but randomized short poems and unanswerable questions. The work offers a cultural critique of modern society’s state of constant suspension, where individuals are trapped in cycles of expectation, endlessly waiting for digital responses or futures that never arrive.

The project investigates the face as both an interface of identity and a target of surveillance. Audiences encounter a material wall of anonymously 3D-printed faces. A camera captures the viewers’ own faces, processing them through AI diffusion models to mutate their features. This algorithmic double is then projected onto the 3D wall. The installation offers a socio-political critique of modern surveillance and reveals how AI models, driven by biased training data, silently recode human subjects.

artists: Kedi Dong (CN), Zhuli Pan (CN), Lisha Zhang (CN)
descEn: The project investigates the dynamic preservation of cultural heritage. Audiences experience an interactive installation where their physical movements unfold layers of evolving digital imagery. Reimagining the ceremonial ephemerality of traditional paper craft, the visuals respond directly to the viewers’ gestures. Culturally, the work draws from Hong Kong’s Cheung Chau Bun Festival, allowing collective memory to be refolded and transforming static folklore into a living digital organism.

The project investigates whether human loss retains meaning when emotions become computable. Audiences will watch a 20-minute AIGC-generated short film depicting a teenage girl and an AI companion as they navigate their way through a period of mourning. Culturally rooted in Guangdong’s 49-day mourning rituals, the work critiques a socio-scientific future where AI systems manage emotional regulation, exploring how technology reconstructs and amplifies the inherent instability of human memory and grief.

In 2025, global military spending reached a record high of 2.9 trillion US dollars, rising for the eleventh consecutive year (SIPRI Military Expenditure Database 2026). At the same time, hard-won progress in equality, climate action and social infrastructure is coming under increasing pressure. War and militarization also serve as political excuses for sidelining urgent social questions. This is exactly where Flood the Zone with Courage begins: on Linz’s Main Square, where new forms of protest emerging from artistic practice meet research and civic engagement, and where it becomes apparent tha

nameEn: Ludwig Boltzmann Gesellschaft—Open Innovation in Science Center
descEn:
The way we think about health is less straightforward than it seems. It is shaped by scientific knowledge, cultural values, lived experience and ongoing societal negotiations—and it evolves with every new technological development.
With the emergence of Artificial Intelligence, the question is no longer what becomes medically possible, but also how AI is changing our understanding of health itself. Between bodies and data, professional judgment and algorithmic recommendation, care and efficiency, lived experience and standardized knowledge, fundamental questions arise: What forms of knowledge

little joys create space to pause, draw breath and take a break from all the negative news which accumulates daily. It is a collection of real, small moments of joy, gathered from the artist's friends and from her own daily life. Such moments can be easily missed when everything else feels so heavy. The artwork carries a simple message: that noticing what makes each day and our (inner) world a little lighter is, over time, a practice worth keeping.

The project explores the boundary between physical presence and spatial memory: How do individuals leave their mark within a tracked, collective ecosystem? The audience enters a pitch-black shapeless labyrinth, where UV lights and interactive projections show the world of illusions. Looking for their own way among apparent walls, hidden rooms and traces left by previous visitors, everyone will find the solution in their own way. Behind the scenes, a distributed network of sensors, AIs, projectors and real-time movement trackers, challenges the visitor armed only with a marker to draw. In an er

The event turns the space into a giant cup of bubble tea, where audiences become tapioca pearls inside a shifting virtual drink. Through movement, disturbance and connection, they collectively brew a constantly changing milk tea. With interactive projection, sensing and real-time animation, Bubble Tea reimagines Taiwan’s iconic drink culture as a playful system of cultural collision, social exchange and shared transformation.

nameEn: Sonic Saturday: Audible Futures, Silent Decisions
descEn:
Since 2016, Anton Bruckner University (ABU) has been hosting the Sonic Saturday as part of the Ars Electronica Festival. The event features spatial sound concerts, live performances, and audiovisual and sound installations. We aim to bring together artists, researchers and an audience interested in electroacoustic music, sonic art, spatial audio and multimedia practices to allow for an informal, in-person exchange of ideas.

Inspired by the festival theme Negotiating Humanity – Future Begins, we consider how the future takes form within sonic practices.

The European Media Art Platform EMAP Extended invites artists, curators and partners to a Get Together. The event brings together members of the 16-organization consortium behind EMAP’s residency program, and offers an opportunity to meet former and current artists in residence as well as partners and to discuss developments in the fields of media art, bioart and robotic art across Europe.

ticket: Ars Electronica Center Ticket, DAYPASS, FESTIVALPASS, FESTIVALPASS+
descEn: Find out what Artificial Intelligence is, what applications already exist and what these are already capable of. This exhibition, for example, demonstrates the structure of neural networks and offers the opportunity for visitors to train these networks themselves through numerous interactive stations.

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn: The interweaving of different knowledge cultures is a central approach for the Ars Electronica Labs. Find out how citizens are actively involved in shaping our world, how the human body can be extended by means of technology, how (new) materials are used to innovatively produce things and how the smallest biological structures and processes shape our lives.

ticket: Ars Electronica Center Ticket, DAYPASS, FESTIVALPASS, FESTIVALPASS+
descEn: Connections between biological systems and artificial technologies help us to better understand the functions of our brain. The brain-computer interface has the potential to improve the rehabilitation of neurological patients.

nameEn: Brunch at the Tangible Music Lab, Tabakfabrik Linz
descEn:
The doors of the Tangible Music Lab will be open for those attending this year’s Ars Electronica Festival. Visitors will have the opportunity to explore experimental musical interfaces, interactive instruments and current research projects. If you are interested in visiting us, we will prepare some demos, snacks and drinks on Saturday, September 12th from 11:00 until 14:00 at the Tangible Music Lab location at the Tabakfabrik Linz. 

How to get there: 
Tangible Music Lab - Institute of Media Studies 
University of Arts Linz 
Peter-Behrens-Platz 8-9, 4020 Linz, Austria

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn: This is the world premiere of the newest artwork from Sputniko!, commissioned by Julius Baer Bank in collaboration with Ars Electronica. In this installation, an evolving panoramic dusk sky overflows with signs and symbols of good fortune drawn from East Asian tradition, inviting us to question the dissolving boundary between authenticity and fabrication in an age of AI-generated worlds.

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn: The use of space has become an increasingly important subject in recent decades. Space for All demonstrates how developments in space are linked to social, technological and artistic perspectives on Earth.

ticket: FESTIVALPASS+, FESTIVALPASS, DAYPASS, Ars Electronica Center Ticket
descEn: Young visitors have time and space to play and discover in our Kids’ Research Laboratory. Whether digital, analog, natural or artificial—for children, the world is a single laboratory in which every moment can become an experiment and every path a journey of discovery.

nameEn: The Syntax of Nature and Other Approximate Truths
descEn: The Syntax of Nature and Other Approximate Truths questions the status of truths commonly regarded as natural and universal. In a world increasingly shaped by algorithms and computational models, the boundary between discovering and constructing reality becomes ever more blurred. The work oscillates between the organic and the synthetic, the human and the generated, exploring a space in which the notions of origin and originality begin to dissolve. At the same time, it acts as a provocation—an impulse to break free from systems of rules in defense of intuition, instinct and epiphany.

The eponymous composition UN-ORGANIC unfolds as an unstable ecology of drifting filaments, luminous spores, vaporous tissues and half-formed organisms. Matter hovers between dead and alive: it breathes without permission, leaks, sends signals through membranes and withdraws into shadow. Familiar divisions between organic and inorganic, natural and artificial collapse into a speculative zone of latent life, nonhuman agencies and perception caught in the undergrowth of machines.

NEKRO//MAKINA is an audiovisual ritual in which death is no longer treated as an ending, but as a state that remains active. Sound and image are bound together within a system that persists beyond collapse, continuously shifting between control and rupture, density and erosion. A fixed audiovisual core provides structure and duration, while live electronic interventions introduce instability, friction and excess. Suspended between ritual and machine, NEKRO//MAKINA inhabits a post-terminal condition where endings have already occurred, yet the apparatus continues to operate.

Drawing upon the four compositions that form Random Check 8, the multimedia installation unfolds as a dynamic field of sound, image and bodily presence. Through choreographic actions and the energy generated by performers and audience alike, it continuously reconfigures the relationships between organic and synthetic forms, inviting participants into a process of transformation, reciprocity and emergence.

descEn: Interface Cultures students are also taking part in this year’s Flood the Zone with Courage program at Linz’s Main Square. They are presenting projects that answer the program’s call for artists, activists, students and citizens to develop new forms of protest—performative, participatory and radically collective.

Both exhibits CAM Trails and tot–M2 explore how technological constraints can become a core part of game design. While CAM Trails uses the slow refresh and visual artifacts of an e-ink display to create tension and shape its narrative, tot–M2 reimagines handheld gaming through tactile interaction and an asynchronous multiplayer. Together, the projects demonstrate how hardware and interface design can influence storytelling, play and new forms of social connection.

nameEn: I Tell the Moon My Secret and the Moon Tells Me Yours
descEn: This interactive artwork explores digital communication shaped by forces beyond human control. Visitors whisper secrets that are translated into robotic movements and long-exposure photographs with the Moon as the sole light source. The project combines robotics, photography and the environment to transform secrets into cryptic visual traces, reflecting on human relationships with technology, nature and uncertainty. The Moon is an active participant rather than a passive object of observation.

BruSHŪ is a sensor-embedded calligraphy brush and real-time cross-modal feedback system. It captures implicit micro-actions during brushwork—contact boundaries, orientation shifts, motion energy—and translates them into synchronized sound and generative visual output. The system operates as a closed sensing-to-feedback loop with no pre-recorded content; all output is generated in real time from live brush movement.

Blending art and science, this installation uses a hybrid media approach, using real-time eye-tracking to connect human perception with cosmic and geological phenomena. A wearable eye tracker maps viewers’ gaze onto a simulation of 64,000 astronomical bodies shaped by dark matter and dark energy, while also shaping projected geological textures derived from an abandoned quarry in China. Integrating astronomy, computation and geology, the work renders invisible planetary forces tangible.

KARMA is a multi-channel audiovisual installation exploring generative AI through the artist’s concept of sensory projection, in which generation is understood as the collapse of countless high-dimensional possibilities into perceptible forms by human intent. Combining real footage with AI-generated imagery, the work unfolds as a shifting field of imagined realities, inviting viewers into an embodied, spatialized encounter with algorithmic perception and the boundaries between the real and the possible.

Touch Our Scar is a tactile, interactive artwork examining trauma as an embodied, non-linguistic experience through “painful weaving”, in which hostile materials are woven into textile forms. Nine individual trauma textiles prompt touch, while two collective textile works detect and respond to contact, evolving in real time as trauma manifests, is processed, and is transformed between body, material and time.

Drawing on Deleuze and Guattari’s concept of “becoming-animal”, the artist presents transformation as an intensification of identity and capacity, always collective, always entangled with forces beyond the individual. AI generation and 3D printing participate actively in this process, distributing agency across algorithms, text, machines and matter, creating a non-human approach to becoming.

A murmuration is a stunning natural phenomenon where thousands of birds form complex, organism-like shapes in the sky. This project explores how relatively simple rules create such collective behavior. Visitors can interact with the flock: the first person becomes the attractor, guiding the flock, while others act as birds of prey, disrupting the swarm and causing ripples. Such emergent behaviors highlight both the vital connectivity but also the fragility of the ecosystems all around us.

Visible from afar, the LED façade of the Ars Electronica Center dominates the townscape of Linz. But this iconic landmark is much more than just eye-catching architecture. Using the local Wi-Fi, visitors can connect to the building with their own smartphones, play music and control the façade’s more than 40,000 LEDs in real time. The Ars Electronica Center thus becomes an instrument that users can play—and the city a shared, luminous creative space.

This project explores a perspective that the artists call “picknick approach”. With it they have created an artwork where visitors interact by simply being present. Visitors are invited to sit down by a bench-icon appearing at their position. The sound of wind is accompanied by colorful leaves that were collected and scanned by the artists floating down the screen. They float by every visitor and when they do, different windharp sounds are heard, creating an atmospheric soundscape.

descEn:
The Lightness of Submission is an interactive kinetic installation in which buoyant robotic agents walk within a circular boundary created entirely by vortex air currents from surrounding fans. Although no physical barrier exists, the agents stay confined within it, colliding and changing direction as they negotiate the forces upon them.
